items.stem: Market interest rates rise after you buy a fixed-coupon bond. All else equal, the bond's market price will:

options.rationale: Correct: bond prices move inversely to market yields.
Prices fall, not rise, when yields increase.
The price adjusts so its yield matches the market.

options.text: Rise then return to par immediately
options.rationale: There is no such automatic snap-back; price simply falls.

items.explanation: Correct: bond prices move inversely to market yields.

items.stem: Which two features generally increase a bond's interest-rate sensitivity (duration)? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Correct: a lower coupon raises duration.

items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: A bond is callable by the issuer. This feature is generally a disadvantage to the holder because:

options.text: The issuer tends to call it when rates fall, forcing reinvestment at lower yields
options.rationale: Correct: calls happen in the holder's least favourable scenario.

options.text: It raises the bond's credit rating automatically
options.rationale: A call feature does not improve credit quality.

options.text: It guarantees a higher coupon for life
options.rationale: The call can end the coupon stream early.
Call features do not eliminate default risk.

items.explanation: Correct: calls happen in the holder's least favourable scenario.
